strengths: Significance: The paper addresses a useful problem in multi-task RL post-training: differing rates of zero-advantage prompts can distort the task mixture after filtering. Figures 3 and 6 provide concrete evidence of this effect.

Originality: Combining reward- and improvement-based task weighting with acceptance-aware batch construction is a practical adaptation of established multi-task optimization ideas to GRPO. The sampler is a potentially useful contribution even independently of the theoretical formulation.

Empirical merits: In the three-task setting, MT-GRPO improves worst-task accuracy from DAPO’s 52.6% to 58.8%, while increasing average accuracy from 65.2% to 66.9%. The task-weight trajectories and sampling diagnostics help explain these gains.

Presentation and ethics: The method’s motivation and component structure are generally clear, and Appendix D provides substantial training details. The experiments use existing synthetic reasoning datasets and an open model; no material research-ethics concern is evident.
weaknesses: Soundness—central objective is incorrect: Equation (5) is not equivalent to the disparity-constrained problem in Equation (4). With the stated negative regularization sign, its inner minimum is exactly min_k J_k(theta) − epsilon(K−1): every simplex vertex has Omega(z)=K−1, and choosing the lowest-reward vertex attains the global lower bound. Thus epsilon does not control a robustness–average-performance trade-off at all. Appendix B.1 also uses the wrong Lagrangian sign for the stated max–min formulation and assumes nonnegative task weights from a mapping that only guarantees their sum is one. These errors invalidate a central claimed contribution.

Soundness—the update guarantees are overstated: Appendix B.3 motivates a local surrogate rather than showing that Algorithm 1 optimizes Equation (5) or prevents weight collapse. Equation (39) also substitutes gamma_t I_k where Equation (32) implies I_k/gamma_t. A constant scaling can be absorbed into tuning parameters, but the derivation should be corrected and its connection to the actual AdamW updates and clipped improvement signals established.

Evidence contradicts broad performance claims: In Figure 7, lambda=1.2 increases worst-task accuracy from 40.9% to 46.3% but reduces average accuracy from 68.7% to 61.7%. Conversely, lambda=0.1 improves average accuracy but lowers worst-task accuracy to 40.4%. These are legitimate trade-offs, but they do not support repeated claims of consistently improving worst-task performance without sacrificing average performance.

Component attribution is incomplete: Figure 10 shows that regularized reward-only weighting achieves 58.4% worst-task and 69.7% average accuracy, compared with 58.8% and 66.9% for improvement-aware weighting at lambda=0.25. This is a strong simpler alternative. Figure 8 mainly reports sampling diagnostics rather than final performance ablations. A controlled comparison of uniform weighting plus ratio preservation, reward-only weighting, and improvement-aware weighting is needed to establish the benefit of the proposed combination.

Efficiency is not established in compute terms: Fewer optimization steps do not imply lower training cost when methods generate and discard different numbers of rollouts. The proposed sampler uses threefold oversampling and up to ten resampling rounds in Experiment 1. Generated-token counts, GPU-hours, or wall-clock comparisons at matched accuracy are needed to substantiate the broader efficiency claim.

Reproducibility and statistical reliability are insufficient: Section 6 reports 10,000 training examples per difficulty, whereas Appendix D reports 1,000. The abstract’s 'Code:' field has no link. Training seed counts, uncertainty estimates, evaluation decoding details, and checkpoint-selection procedures are not adequately specified. With only 200 evaluation instances per task, uncertainty is especially relevant to smaller differences and worst-task selection. The estimation of task rewards and improvements, including handling tasks absent from a batch, also needs clarification.

Scope and limitations: All experiments use Qwen-2.5-3B and three synthetic task families; the nine-task setting expands difficulty levels rather than introducing six new task families. This can support a specialized contribution, but provides limited evidence for general-purpose reasoning reliability. Moreover, Algorithm 2 can miss requested task proportions after exhausting its resampling budget, so claims that it guarantees faithful proportions should be qualified and accompanied by measured mismatch rates.

strengths: Significance: Task-dependent filtering rates are a useful practical concern in multi-task GRPO. Figures 3 and 6 illustrate how filtering changes the task composition of training batches, motivating explicit control of accepted samples.

Empirical merits: In the three-task experiment, MT-GRPO improves worst-task accuracy from DAPO’s 52.6% to 58.8%, while increasing average accuracy from 65.2% to 66.9%. These results suggest that the proposed combination can be practically useful.

Originality: Combining reward-based and improvement-based task weighting with acceptance-aware sampling is a plausible adaptation of established multi-task optimization ideas to RL post-training. The contribution is primarily this integration and its empirical diagnosis.

Presentation and reproducibility: The manuscript provides readable algorithm descriptions, training-dynamics plots, regularization comparisons, and substantial hyperparameter and hardware details in Appendix D. Section 6.2 explicitly acknowledges the observed robustness–average-performance trade-off. No material research-ethics concern is apparent from the described experiments.
weaknesses: Soundness—central objective is incorrect: Equation (5) is not equivalent to the disparity-constrained problem in Equation (4). For the stated regularizer and any ε ≥ 0, its inner minimum equals min_k J_k(θ) − ε(K−1): the objective is concave in z and a minimizing vertex has Ω(z)=K−1. Thus ε only adds a constant and cannot control the claimed robustness–average-performance trade-off. At ε=0, maximizing minimum reward also does not enforce equal task rewards. Appendix B.1 uses the wrong Lagrangian sign for the stated max–min formulation and does not justify restricting the induced coefficients to nonnegative simplex weights. This undermines a central theoretical contribution.

Soundness—the implemented update lacks the claimed connection to that objective: Appendix B.3 derives a separate local surrogate, without establishing equivalence to Equation (5) or showing that the practical update prevents weight collapse. Equation (39) also uses γ_t I_k where Equation (32) implies I_k/γ_t. A constant scaling can be absorbed into tuning, but the derivation needs correction, and the guarantees should be distinguished from heuristic motivation.

Soundness—ratio preservation is overstated: Matching accepted prompt counts does not establish matching contributions to the original expected policy gradient. If task k has acceptance probability p_k and rejected samples have zero gradient, its conditional accepted gradient is E[g_k]/p_k. Sampling accepted tasks in proportions z_k therefore generally changes the effective weighting of the unfiltered objective. Algorithm 2 also allows unmet task quotas when its resampling budget expires. The paper should state precisely what is preserved and qualify its objective-alignment claims.

Evidence and claim calibration: Figure 7 does not support consistently improving worst-task accuracy without sacrificing average performance. At λ=0.1, worst-task accuracy is 40.4%, below DAPO’s 40.9%. At λ=1.2, it rises to 46.3%, but average accuracy falls from 68.7% to 61.7%, and average relative change is −7.7%. This can be a useful trade-off, but the broad claims in the introduction and algorithm discussion overstate the results.

Evaluation and attribution: Experiments use one 3B model and three synthetic task families; the nine-task setting consists of difficulty variants of those same families. No seed counts or uncertainty estimates are reported. The sampler ablations mainly measure batch composition and resampling rounds rather than downstream accuracy. Moreover, Figure 10 shows reward-only regularized weighting reaching 58.4% worst-task and 69.7% average accuracy, versus 58.8% and 66.9% for improvement-aware weighting. Consequently, the added value of the improvement signal is less decisive than claimed.

Efficiency: Fewer optimizer steps do not establish lower computational cost when the method oversamples and regenerates rollouts. Appendix D permits an oversampling factor of three and up to ten resampling rounds in Experiment 1. Generated-token counts, GPU-hours, or comparisons at matched rollout budgets are needed to substantiate the broader efficiency claim.

Reproducibility and limitations: Section 6 specifies 10,000 training instances per difficulty, whereas Appendix D specifies 1,000. Evaluation decoding, aggregation, checkpoint selection, and hyperparameter-selection procedures are insufficiently specified. It is also unclear whether task rewards are estimated before or after filtering and how absent tasks are handled during weight updates. These gaps, together with limited experimental scope and unresolved theoretical errors, prevent reliable acceptance despite the promising empirical idea.

strengths: Significance: The paper addresses a useful problem: average performance can conceal weak tasks, and filtering uninformative rollouts can distort the intended training mixture. Explicitly tracking task proportions after filtering is a practical contribution to multi-task RL post-training.

Empirical merits: In the three-task setting, MT-GRPO improves worst-task accuracy from DAPO's 52.6% to 58.8%, while increasing average accuracy from 65.2% to 66.9%. The task-weight and batch-composition plots provide useful evidence about the proposed mechanism.

Originality: Although robust task weighting and improvement-based optimization have established precedents, their combination with acceptance-aware sampling addresses a concrete complication of GRPO. The sampler ablations and reward-only reweighting comparisons help investigate this adaptation.

Presentation and reproducibility: The main narrative is accessible, with informative training-dynamics plots and substantial algorithmic detail. Appendix D specifies hardware, optimizer settings, rollout counts, rewards, and sampling hyperparameters. The synthetic, verifiable reasoning tasks raise no apparent material research-ethics concerns.
weaknesses: Soundness—central objective: Equation (5) is not equivalent to the disparity-constrained problem in Equation (4). Its negative regularization term rewards departures from uniformity in the inner minimization. In fact, with the stated regularizer, the inner optimum is exactly min_k J_k(theta) minus epsilon times (K−1): every simplex vertex has regularizer K−1, and a vertex corresponding to the worst task attains the lower bound. Thus epsilon cannot control the claimed robustness–average trade-off. Appendix B.1 also uses the wrong Lagrangian sign for a maximization problem with upper-bound constraints and infers simplex membership from weights summing to one without establishing nonnegativity. These errors invalidate a central theoretical claim.

Soundness—connection to the algorithm: Appendix B.3 motivates a separate local gradient-balancing objective, but does not establish that improvement-aware updates optimize Equation (5) or prevent weight collapse. Equation (39) also substitutes gamma_t times I_k where Equation (32) implies I_k divided by gamma_t. Constant rescaling could be absorbed into tuning, but the claimed derivation needs correction. Moreover, preserving accepted sample counts does not by itself preserve gradients of the original task objectives: conditioning on acceptance changes each task's expected gradient by its acceptance rate, even when rejected samples have zero gradient.

Empirical claims exceed the results: In Figure 7, lambda=0.1 gives worst-task accuracy of 40.4%, below DAPO's 40.9%. At lambda=1.2, the improvement to 46.3% comes with average accuracy falling from 68.7% to 61.7%. This is a meaningful trade-off, but does not support an unqualified claim of consistently improving worst-task performance without sacrificing average performance. Figure 10 also shows that simpler regularized reward-only weighting achieves 58.4% worst-task accuracy and 69.7% average accuracy, making the necessity of the improvement signal less convincing.

Evaluation and attribution: All experiments use one 3B model and three synthetic task families; the nine-task experiment adds difficulty levels rather than new families. No seed counts, uncertainty estimates, or confidence intervals are reported, despite only 200 evaluation instances per variant. Figure 8 measures batch ratios and resampling rounds, but does not report downstream accuracy for the sampler ablations, leaving its contribution to the final gains insufficiently isolated.

Efficiency: Fewer optimizer steps do not establish lower computational cost. MT-GRPO oversamples and may perform multiple regeneration rounds, with task-dependent response lengths and acceptance rates. Generated-token counts, GPU-hours, or wall-clock comparisons are needed to substantiate practical efficiency; fewer resampling rounds alone are insufficient.

Reproducibility and limitations: Section 6 reports 10,000 training instances per difficulty level, whereas Appendix D reports 1,000. The manuscript leaves unclear the evaluation decoding and checkpoint-selection protocol, whether reweighting rewards are measured before or after filtering, how filtering-rate estimates are updated, and precisely how improvement clipping is applied. Algorithm 2 also does not specify the filtering-rate output required by Algorithm 1. These omissions, together with the limited discussion of generalization and compute costs, make reliable reproduction and interpretation difficult.

strengths: Significance: The paper addresses a useful problem in multi-task RL post-training: average performance can conceal weak tasks, and task-dependent filtering can distort the intended training mixture. The diagnostics in Figures 3, 6, and 16 make this failure mode concrete.

Originality: Combining reward-based task weighting, improvement signals, and acceptance-aware batch construction is a useful adaptation of existing robust and multi-task optimization ideas to GRPO. The distinction between task rewards and the GRPO surrogate loss is particularly relevant.

Empirical merits: The three-task experiment improves worst-task accuracy from DAPO’s 52.6% to 58.8%, with average accuracy increasing from 65.2% to 66.9%. Evaluation extends to Qwen2.5-7B and OLMo-3-7B, and includes component ablations, sequential-training comparisons, and simpler regularized weighting.

Presentation and practical evaluation: The main algorithm is understandable, and task-weight and batch-composition plots help explain its behavior. Appendix D.5 measures actual wall-clock performance and acknowledges the sampler’s 10.2% per-step overhead. The limitations appropriately distinguish robustness within the training mixture from generalization to unseen tasks.
weaknesses: Soundness—objective-to-algorithm gap: Equation (5) is explicitly a simplex-restricted surrogate of the disparity-constrained problem, so it does not enforce Equation (4)’s guarantees. More importantly, the implemented improvement-aware update follows a different local objective in Equation (33), without establishing a relationship between its lambda and Equation (5)’s epsilon. Claims that the method optimizes the stated robustness objective or prevents weight collapse therefore exceed the analysis. Appendix C.3 also incorrectly substitutes gamma_t times I_k for an inner product that Equation (32) implies is approximately I_k divided by gamma_t; constant rescaling can accommodate this operationally, but the derivation needs correction.

Soundness—sampling claims are too strong: Preserving accepted prompt counts does not establish equivalence to the original weighted task gradients. If task k has acceptance probability a_k and rejected samples have zero gradient, its unconditional expected gradient is a_k times its conditional accepted gradient. Sampling accepted tasks in proportions z_k therefore changes the effective objective unless this conditioning is incorporated explicitly. Furthermore, Algorithm 2 can exhaust its resampling budget and fill remaining slots from other tasks, so exact ratio preservation is not guaranteed.

Evidence and reproducibility: No repeated-seed results, uncertainty intervals, or sufficiently detailed evaluation decoding protocol are reported. With 200 evaluation instances per task, uncertainty matters for several incremental gains. Appendix D.1 selects each OLMo method’s best-worst-task checkpoint without specifying an independent validation set. Section 6 reports 10,000 training instances per task difficulty, whereas Appendix E reports 1,000. The promised code link is absent, and the 7B dataset splits and training configurations are insufficiently specified.

Significance and claim calibration: Improvements do not consistently preserve average performance. In the nine-task setting, lambda=1.2 raises worst-task accuracy from 40.9% to 46.3% while reducing average accuracy from 68.7% to 61.7%; lambda=0.1 slightly lowers worst-task accuracy. For Qwen2.5-7B, the largest robustness gain lowers average accuracy from 58.3% to 51.8%. These are potentially useful trade-offs, but they contradict unqualified claims of consistent robustness improvements without sacrificing average performance.

Attribution of gains: Figure 20 shows that simpler regularized reward-only weighting achieves 58.4% worst-task and 69.7% average accuracy, versus 58.8% and 66.9% for improvement-aware weighting. Without uncertainty estimates and comparably tuned trade-off curves, the necessity and added value of the improvement signal remain unclear. Reproducing that signal also requires clarification of the fixed rollout/advantage convention, missing-task handling, and the ambiguous instruction that improvements are clipped to {0.1, 0.2}.

Research ethics: The impact statement’s assertion that improving reasoning entails no potential unethical applications is unjustified. A proportionate discussion should acknowledge dual-use capability improvements and distinguish benchmark balance from demonstrated reliability in healthcare, legal, or other high-stakes deployment. This is secondary to the technical and evidential concerns driving rejection.

strengths: Significance: The paper addresses a useful problem in multi-task RL post-training: unequal rates of uninformative rollout groups can distort task proportions after filtering. Explicitly balancing accepted samples is a practical contribution.

Empirical evidence: Improvements extend beyond the initial synthetic setting to Qwen2.5-7B and OLMo-3-7B. Reported worst-task gains are substantial: 58.8% versus DAPO’s 52.6% in Experiment 1, and 37.6% versus 25.0% in the heterogeneous Qwen-7B experiment.

Evaluation: The appendix includes component ablations, regularized reward-only alternatives, sequential-training comparisons, and actual wall-clock measurements. Table 1 supports an efficiency benefit despite the reported 10.2% per-step overhead; the evidence is not limited to counting optimization steps.

Presentation and originality: The central filtering problem is clearly illustrated, and combining improvement-aware weighting with acceptance-aware batch construction is a useful adaptation of established robust and multi-task optimization ideas. The limitations appropriately acknowledge restriction to the training mixture and verifiable rewards.
weaknesses: Soundness—objective and algorithm are insufficiently connected. Equation (5) is explicitly a simplex-restricted surrogate of the disparity-constrained problem, so it does not enforce Equation (4)’s constraints. More importantly, the implemented improvement-aware update follows the different local objective in Appendix C.3, without establishing a relationship between its lambda and Equation (5)’s epsilon. Claims that the algorithm optimizes the proposed robustness objective or prevents weight collapse are therefore stronger than the analysis supports. Equation (39) also reverses the learning-rate scaling implied by Equation (32): the inner product should approximate I/gamma, not gamma I.

Soundness—preserving accepted-sample proportions is not equivalent to preserving the original task-gradient contributions. If task k has acceptance probability a_k and rejected groups have zero policy gradient, its original expected gradient is a_k times the conditional accepted-group gradient. Sampling accepted groups in proportion z_k instead produces weights proportional to z_k/a_k relative to that original objective. This may be a useful algorithm, but the manuscript needs to state the changed objective rather than claim faithful realization of the original weighted gradients. Finite resampling budgets and the fallback in Algorithm 2 also mean target proportions are not guaranteed.

Reproducibility has material gaps. Section 6 reports 10,000 training instances per difficulty, whereas Appendix E reports 1,000. Appendix E describes all experiments as Qwen-3B runs of 720 steps, leaving the 7B experiments without comparably complete configurations. The code-availability sentence has no link. It is also unclear whether task rewards are estimated before or after filtering, how absent tasks in a batch are handled, and exactly how pre/post-update improvement is evaluated with fixed rollouts and advantages. These choices directly affect the proposed weighting mechanism.

Statistical reliability is unestablished. No seed counts, variation across training runs, or confidence intervals are reported, despite evaluation sets of only 200 instances per task in the controlled experiments. Evaluation decoding, lambda selection, and validation/test separation for checkpoint selection are insufficiently specified. Appendix D.1 selects each method’s best-worst-task checkpoint without explaining an independent selection set. These omissions particularly matter for smaller gains over stronger ablations.

The evidence for the distinctive improvement-aware component is mixed. In Figure 20, regularized reward-only weighting achieves 58.4% worst-task and 69.7% average accuracy, compared with 58.8% and 66.9% for MT-GRPO at lambda=0.25. Thus, its worst-task advantage is only 0.4 percentage points while average accuracy is lower. Figure 21 shows a trade-off rather than uniform superiority over regularization. The results support useful filtering and reweighting mechanisms, but do not convincingly establish the necessity or consistent advantage of the proposed improvement signal.

Claims about retaining average performance need qualification. In Experiment 2, the highlighted worst-task improvement accompanies an average-accuracy decrease from 68.7% to 61.7%; in Experiment 3, average accuracy decreases from 58.3% to 51.8%. These are legitimate robustness trade-offs, but do not support the introduction’s unqualified 'without sacrificing' language. Likewise, improved minimum benchmark accuracy establishes within-mixture balance, not deployment reliability. The impact statement’s assertion that enhanced reasoning has no potential unethical applications is unjustified, although no concrete ethical violation is demonstrated.

strengths: Significance: The paper addresses a useful problem: improving the weakest tasks during multi-task RL post-training. Task-dependent filtering rates are a concrete obstacle to realizing intended training mixtures, and the proposed sampler directly addresses that obstacle.

Originality: Combining reward- and improvement-based reweighting with acceptance-aware, task-quota sampling is a meaningful adaptation of existing robust and multi-task optimization ideas to GRPO. The contribution is primarily this integration and its empirical analysis.

Empirical evidence: Gains extend beyond the controlled synthetic setting. Worst-task accuracy improves from 52.6% to 58.8% against DAPO in Experiment 1 and from 25.0% to 37.6% on the heterogeneous Qwen2.5-7B mixture. The OLMo experiment provides additional evidence across model families.

Evaluation and presentation: Component ablations, task-weight trajectories, sequential-training comparisons, and regularized reward-only baselines help explain the method. The wall-clock analysis is particularly useful: Appendix D.5 acknowledges 10.2% per-step overhead while demonstrating faster attainment of worst-task accuracy targets. The limitations appropriately acknowledge restriction to the training mixture and verifiable rewards.
weaknesses: Soundness—objective and algorithm are insufficiently connected. Equation (5) is explicitly a simplex-restricted surrogate, so it does not enforce Equation (4)'s disparity constraint; maximizing minimum reward does not imply equal task rewards. More importantly, the implemented improvement-aware update does not optimize Equation (5)'s L1-regularized inner objective. Appendix C.3 derives a different local optimization problem, without establishing a correspondence between lambda and epsilon or proving the claimed prevention of weight collapse. Equation (39) also incorrectly substitutes gamma times improvement where Equation (32) implies improvement divided by gamma. The algorithm may be useful, but the claimed optimization interpretation needs qualification.

Soundness—preserving accepted task counts is not equivalent to preserving the original task gradients. Conditioning on nonzero-advantage groups scales each task's expected reward-surrogate gradient by the inverse of its acceptance probability. Consequently, sampling accepted groups in proportions z generally does not implement Equation (6) for the original prompt distributions without an additional correction or a redefined objective. Algorithm 2 also permits quota violations when regeneration budgets are exhausted. The manuscript should distinguish these effects from exact alignment with intended gradient contributions.

Reproducibility: Appendix E contains an unfinished code-release sentence and contradicts Section 6 on training-set size: 1,000 versus 10,000 instances per difficulty. It also describes all experiments as Qwen-2.5-3B training for 720 steps, leaving the 7B experiments without comparable implementation details. Critical estimator choices remain unclear: whether task rewards are computed before or after filtering, whether improvement uses fixed rollouts and advantages, and how tasks absent from a batch are handled. These choices directly affect the proposed reweighting mechanism.

Evidential strength: No training-seed variability or confidence intervals are reported, despite only 200 evaluation instances per difficulty in the controlled datasets. Evaluation decoding and checkpoint-selection protocols are insufficiently specified; Appendix D.1 selects each method's best-worst-task checkpoint without identifying an independent validation set. These omissions make smaller differences and hyperparameter comparisons difficult to assess reliably.

Claims exceed the demonstrated trade-off. In Experiment 2, increasing worst-task accuracy from DAPO's 40.9% to 46.3% reduces average accuracy from 68.7% to 61.7%; Experiment 3 similarly reduces average accuracy from 58.3% to 51.8%. These are legitimate trade-offs, but do not support repeated claims of avoiding average-performance sacrifice. The necessity of improvement-aware weighting is also not established: Figure 20's regularized reward-only variant achieves 58.4% worst-task and 69.7% average accuracy, versus 58.8% and 66.9% for MT-GRPO, with no uncertainty estimates.

Research ethics: The impact statement's assertion that enhancing reasoning entails no potential unethical applications is unsupported. A proportionate discussion should acknowledge possible misuse and distinguish benchmark task balance from safe deployment in healthcare or legal settings. No concrete ethical violation is apparent, but the current impact discussion is inadequate.
